sections.html:
The family Polynemidae is almost unknown to hobbyists, although 96 species have been described over the centuries, 42 are still valid, and these fish are important food fishes in their home range. Two species of the genus Polynemus have only 7 spines in the first dorsal fin (most species have 8): P. paradiseus, described in 1758 by Linné, and P. hornadyai, described in 1936 by Myers.

The youngsters from Thailand come from aquaculture and are only 6-8 cm long, but the long filaments are much longer than the body including the tail fin. These filaments serve as sensitive organs, comparable to the ventral fins of the gouramis (Colisa and Trichogaster). The filaments originate from the pectoral fins. Maximum length reported for P. polynemus is 30 cm, but only very rarely are specimens longer than 17 cm collected.
P. paradiseus has a very wide distribution along the whole eastern coastline of the Indian subcontinent to Thailand, while P. hornadyai is known so far only from the Malayan part of Borneo.
Basically speaking, Polynemus inhabit river mouths and prefer brackish water.
These fish should be kept in large aquaria with a sandy bottom and as little furnishing as possible; they need free space for swimming.

These fish need high oxygen content and are very sensitive to organic pollution of the water. In the long term they should be kept in strongly brackish water (10-15 g salt/litre) or in pure marine water, although the specimens at the supplier are adapted to pure freshwater.
They feed on small invertebrates. Bloodworm is a perfect food for them.
P. paradiseus is completely peaceful towards conspecifics and other fish, but care must be taken that other fish do not nip at the long filaments.
